title: Dice games
objectives: Value a dice game by expectation, and find the best rule for rerolling.

screens.title: Dice games
screens.prose:
Work these books easiest first:

- Mosteller, *Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability*: dice, matching, stopping
- Zhou, the green book, *A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews*: coins, coupons, cards
- Crack, *Heard on the Street*: quick expected values
- Joshi and co-authors, *Quant Job Interview Questions and Answers*: harder variants
- *Probability and Markets*, a free guide from a trading firm: value as a price

screens.title: Paid the face
screens.prose: We start with the simplest game. You roll a fair die once and are paid £1 for each pip.
screens.question: What is a fair price to play, in £?

hints.text: Each face has chance $\tfrac16$.
Add the payouts in the row and divide by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each face is equally likely: average the six payouts.

byKey.max: You priced the best roll. A 6 comes only one time in six.
byKey.sum: You added the six faces but did not divide by six.

explain.text: $E[X] = (1 + 2 + \dots + 6)/6 = 3.5$. A fair price is the expected payout. Pay more and you lose on average; pay less and the seller does.

screens.title: The larger of two dice
screens.prose: Now roll two dice and be paid the larger face in £. Each cell shows the larger face for one of the 36 equally likely outcomes.
screens.question: Tap every cell where the larger face is 6.

hints.text: Which cells contain a 6 at all?
The bottom row and the right column hold every 6.
Row 6 and column 6 share the double six: $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$ cells.

feedback.correct: Eleven cells: a 6 on either die, with the double six counted once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 6 on either die makes the larger face 6.

byKey.row: You took the cells where the first die is 6. A 6 on the second die counts too.
byKey.col: You took the cells where the second die is 6. A 6 on the first die counts too.

explain.text: The larger face is 6 in $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$ cells. In the same way it is 5 in 9 cells and 4 in 7. Each larger face $m$ fills an L of $2m - 1$ cells.

screens.title: Price the larger
screens.prose: Each larger face $m$ fills $2m - 1$ cells: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 of the 36. The fair price of a game is its **value**: the expected payout.
screens.question: What is the value of the larger-of-two game, in £? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Multiply each face by its number of cells.
The 6 fills 11 cells and contributes $6 \times 11 = 66$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each face $m$ by its $2m - 1$ cells, then divide by 36.

byKey.one: You priced one die. The larger of two is at least as big as either.
byKey.sum: You priced the sum of the dice. The game pays only the larger one.

explain.text: $E[\max] = (1 + 6 + 15 + 28 + 45 + 66)/36 = 161/36 \approx 4.4722$. As a check, the larger and smaller faces add to the total, which averages 7. So the smaller is worth $7 - 4.4722 = 2.5278$.

screens.title: Paying to reroll
screens.prose: A new game. Roll one die and keep the face in £. Or pay £1 to roll again, as often as you like. Call its value $V$. Try the rule: keep 4, 5 or 6, and reroll the rest.
screens.question: Under this rule $V = \tfrac{4 + 5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac{3}{6}(V - 1)$. What is $V$, in £?

hints.text: A reroll pays $V$ again, less the £1.
The three rerolled faces each lead to $V - 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Collect the $V$ terms on one side.

byKey.free: You dropped the £1 a reroll costs. With free rerolls you would wait for a 6, but each try here costs.
byKey.one: That is one roll with no reroll. The option to reroll adds value.

explain.text: The three kept faces give $15/6 = 2.5$, and each reroll restarts the game for £1. Solving $V = 2.5 + \tfrac12(V - 1)$ gives $V = 4$.

screens.title: Is the rule best?
screens.prose: We guessed a rule and found $V = 4$. Now check that no other rule does better.
screens.question: Put the check in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: A reroll costs £1 and restarts the game, so it is worth $V - 1 = 3$.
Faces 4, 5 and 6 beat 3, so keep them.
Face 3 ties with 3, so keeping and rerolling are worth the same.
Faces 1 and 2 lose to 3, so reroll them.
Each face gets its better choice, so $V = E[\max(X, V - 1)] = 4$.
Keep any face above 3.5, the average of one roll.

hints.text: What do you compare each face with?
A reroll is worth $V - 1 = 3$.
Compare 4, 5, 6, then 3, then 1 and 2 with 3, and conclude.

feedback.correct: The rule takes the better of keeping and rerolling on every face, so it is optimal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from what a reroll is worth, then compare each face with it.

byKey.d1: A reroll is not worth 3.5 here. You pay £1 and then play on with your best rule, so it is worth $V - 1$.
byKey.left-out: Every line but one belongs. Only the line about 3.5 is wrong.
byKey.s5: The conclusion comes last, after every face is compared.
byKey.s1: Start with the value of a reroll: every comparison uses it.

explain.text: A rule is best when each face takes the larger of keeping it and $V - 1$. At $V = 4$ that is true for every face, with face 3 indifferent. So $V$ solves $V = E[\max(X, V - 1)]$.

screens.title: Paid the square
screens.prose: One die again, now paid the square of the face in £: a 4 pays £16.
screens.question: What is the fair price?

options.why: You squared the average roll. The mean of a square is not the square of the mean: the 36 pulls the average up.
You averaged the smallest and largest payouts. The squares are not evenly spaced, so their midpoint is not their mean.
You priced the face. The game pays its square.

hints.text: List the six payouts.
They are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and 36.
Their sum is 91, so the price is $91/6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the six squares themselves.

byKey.b: You squared the average roll. Average the squares instead: $(1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6$.

explain.text: $E[X^2] = 91/6 \approx 15.17$, which beats $3.5^2 = 12.25$ by the variance, $35/12$. A payout that grows faster than the face rewards spread. So the square of the mean always undershoots.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose: Every game here was priced the same way. The **value** of a game is the expected payout under your best rule. When you may pay $c$ to start again, $$V = E[\max(X,\, V - c)],$$ so you keep a face exactly when it beats $V - c$.
screens.question: In the reroll game, why compare a face with $V - 1$ and not with 3.5?

options.text: A reroll costs £1 and then lets you play on with the same best rule
3.5 is what a reroll is worth
options.why: That is one roll with no further choice. After a reroll you may reroll again, and each one costs £1.

options.text: The best rule always keeps exactly half the faces
options.why: Half is a coincidence here. With a £0.50 cost you would keep 5 and 6, and be indifferent at 4.

feedback.correct: Yes. A reroll restarts the whole game, less its cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what you hold after paying for a reroll.

explain.text: After paying £1 you face the same game again, worth $V$. So a reroll is worth $V - 1$, and every face is compared with that.

screens.title: A price on the spot
screens.prose: A market-making interviewer asks for a market on the larger of two dice, settled in £. You have a few seconds to quote a bid and an offer.
screens.question: Which quote is centred on fair value?

options.why: You quoted one die. The larger of two is worth $161/36 \approx$ £4.47.
You priced the sum of the dice. The bet pays only the larger face.
You guessed the larger face is usually 5 or 6. That happens in 20 of 36 cells, and the average is £4.47.

hints.text: What is the larger of two dice worth?
Each face $m$ fills $2m - 1$ cells; you found $161/36$.
$161/36 \approx 4.47$; choose the quote that straddles it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the value first, then pick the market around it.

byKey.b: You quoted one die. A buyer at £3.60 gets £4.47 on average from you.

explain.text: A market straddles the value, so you buy below it and sell above it. Say the method as you quote: face $m$ fills $2m - 1$ of 36 cells. The interviewer hears a price and a reason.

ideas: The value of a game is its expected payout under your best rule.
Shade the 36 cells by the payout and count: the larger face $m$ fills $2m - 1$ cells.
With a paid reroll, keep a face exactly when it beats $V - c$, and solve $V = E[\max(X, V - c)]$.

formula.name: Value of a reroll game
formula.note: Keep a face when it beats $V - c$.

summary.trap: Pricing the square of a die at $3.5^2$. The mean of a square is not the square of the mean.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice, paid the smaller face in £.
quiz.question: What is the fair price? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The smaller face is $m$ in $13 - 2m$ cells, or use the larger face.

byKey.one: That is one die. The smaller of two is at most either die.
byKey.larger: That is the larger face. The game pays the smaller.

explain.text: The larger and the smaller add to the total, which averages 7. So $E[\min] = 7 - 161/36 = 91/36 \approx 2.5278$.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice, paid the absolute difference of the faces in £.
quiz.question: What is the fair price? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells with difference 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

byKey.zero: You took the difference of the averages, $3.5 - 3.5$. The average of a difference in size is not the difference of averages.
byKey.half: You averaged 0 to 5 as if each were equally likely. A small difference fills more cells.

quiz.prose: Roll a fair die until the first 6. You are paid the sum of all the faces, the 6 included.
quiz.question: What is the fair price, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the expected number of rolls, then the average face.

byKey.count: That is the expected number of rolls. The game pays their sum.

explain.text: The number of rolls averages 6 and each face averages 3.5, so the sum averages $6 \times 3.5 = 21$. As a check, five non-six rolls average 3 each, then the 6: $15 + 6 = 21$.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice, paid the product of the faces in £.
quiz.question: What is the fair price?

options.why: That is the average square of one die. Two different dice are independent, so the means multiply.

options.text: It needs all 36 products added up
options.why: Adding all 36 works but is slow. For independent dice the mean of the product is the product of the means.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The dice are independent.

byKey.b: One die squared is $X \cdot X$, which is not independent of itself. Two dice are.

explain.text: Independence gives $E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] = 12.25$. This is the edge case of the square trap: there the two factors were the same die.
